awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Turmeric Assisted Pressure Sterilization
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impacts of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project would be two-fold: potential reduction of packaged Ready-to-Eat (RTE) food waste, and broader availability of packaged food in its original taste, flavor, and nutrients. The amount of food wasted in the U.S. annually is equivalent to 130 billion meals, with an approximate value of nearly $218 billion. A significant percentage of this food waste happens in the fresh/produce section of the supermarkets due to the shorter shelf-life of various food items from 10 to 30 days. These foods are typically processed via retort cooking at 250-degree F, or freezing, or making food acidic (below Ph 4.6). These technologies are energy consuming, expensive, and lead to loss of most of the nutrients. The proposed Turmeric Assisted Pressure Sterilization (TAPS) is aiming to be the first technology that can extend this shelf-life to over 180 days without compromising on original taste, flavor and nutrient of food items with the goal of bringing RTE food items from the colder sections of the supermarket (below 40-degree F) to the shelf-stable section (about 70-degree F). By doing so, the company aspires to reduce RTE food waste by 20% in the next 10 years. 


This SBIR Phase I project aims to lay the groundwork for establishing TAPS as a breakthrough pressure sterilization technology. Traditional pressure sterilization is carried out at pressures around 6000 bars and 40-degree F.  This project intends to show that in the presence of natural antioxidants such as turmeric, the same level of sterilization can be achieved at pressures close to 3000 bar and 70-degree F. The project, therefore, will focus on preparing and testing a variety of RTE foods under the TAPS conditions and assessing their efficacy by third-party for shelf life, nutrient preservation, and risks to food safety and quality when challenged with common microorganisms. Besides turmeric, the experiments will also involve the use of other natural antioxidants, including a commercially available curcuminoid extract that has enhanced bioavailability and stability compared to standard curcumin and is colorless, odorless and tasteless, further expanding the potential applicability of TAPS to a much wider range of cuisines.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Fresh, minimally processed foods offer desirable taste, texture, and nutritional qualities, yet their limited shelf life contributes to food waste and restricts distribution. Conventional thermal preservation can extend shelf life but may change sensory characteristics. High-pressure processing (HPP) offers a nonthermal alternative, although pressure alone does not reliably inactivate bacterial spores. Hence, HPP treated foods like fruit juices, hummus, guacamole etc have a refrigerated shelf-life of 50 to 100 days. Turmeric Assisted Pressure Sterilization (TAPS) combines a proprietary antioxidant-based formulation with HPP to kill both bacteria and bacterial spores, extending refrigerated shelf-life to 180 to 500 days while preserving desirable product qualities.

The NSF Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project investigated the technical feasibility and commercial potential of TAPS across four product groups. Independent laboratory shelf-life studies provided evidence of extended product stability and identified promising applications for further validation.

First, prepared meals containing rice, proteins, vegetables and onion, tomato or spinach-based sauces were evaluated for approximately one year under refrigeration. The results support further development of convenient, refrigerated meals with extended shelf life.

Second, a salmon salad containing cooked salmon, mayonnaise, celery, and raw onion was evaluated for more than 100 days under refrigeration. This work extended the TAPS research beyond fully cooked curries to a mixed-ingredient, ready-to-eat refrigerated product. It also explored a curcumin extract as an alternative to turmeric where minimal color, flavor, and aroma are commercially desirable.

Third, onion based, creamy tomato and coconut milk-based sauces packaged in low-oxygen-transmission foil pouches were examined during ambient-temperature storage for up to six months. These observations motivate further research into applications where refrigeration is limited, including disaster response and humanitarian distribution.

Fourth, the project evaluated beverages, including concentrated daily shots, apple juice, mango lassi, and salted lassi. The work investigated antioxidant-rich formulations and oxygen radical absorbance capacity (ORAC) as an analytical measure of antioxidant activity. ORAC results characterize laboratory antioxidant capacity; not the theoretical values from the literature.

Its prior market experience includes progression from Michigan farmers' markets to retail distribution across multiple U.S. states and production activities in Florida and Missouri. The team signed an initial licensing agreement with Nuty Foods, which operates an integrated HPP production facility in Mexico. This relationship may help test whether licensed production can lower manufacturing costs and expand access to competitively priced foods.

The next major challenge is scale. Existing HPP infrastructure is capital-intensive, and global capacity could constrain widespread adoption. A proposed Phase II research direction is to evaluate whether selected TAPS formulations can achieve independently validated microbial-control and shelf-life targets at lower pressures and shorter hold times, enabling more affordable equipment. A target machine cost of approximately $150,000 is an engineering objective, not a demonstrated outcome. This reduction in cost to $150k from present  $1 million for HPP machines has potential to expand HPP footprints from existing 2-3% to 10% in the next 5 years.

Overall, NSF Phase I advanced TAPS from product-level observations toward a broader, evidence-driven technology licensing strategy. The project generated promising shelf-life findings across meals, salads, sauces, and beverages; strengthened customer discovery and intellectual-property positioning; and identified the scientific, regulatory, and equipment-development work needed for commercialization. The long-term goal is to reduce food waste and make safe, nutritious, appealing foods more affordable and accessible.
